sentences: The story begins when the squire of the manor house in the county visits the detective and gives him a piece of paper with the following mysterious sequence of stick figures.
The squire explains to the detective and the companion that he has recently married an American woman, the wife.

Before the wedding, she had asked her husband-to-be never to ask about her past, as she had had some "very disagreeable associations" in her life, although she said that there was nothing that she was personally ashamed of.
Their marriage had been a happy one until the messages began to arrive, first mailed from her homeland and then appearing in the garden.
The messages had made the wife very afraid but she did not explain the reasons for her fear, and the squire insisted on honouring his promise not to ask about the wife's life in her homeland.

The detective examines all of the occurrences of the dancing figures, and they provide him with an important clue—he realises that they form a substitution cipher and cracks the code by frequency analysis.
The last of the messages causes the detective to fear that the squire and his wife are in immediate danger.
The detective rushes to the manor house and finds the squire dead of a bullet to the heart and his wife gravely wounded from a gunshot to the head.
The local inspector of the county constabulary believes that it is a murder-suicide attempt; the wife is the prime suspect.
But the detective, after noting some inconsistencies in that theory, proves that there is a third person involved.
The detective writes a message—in dancing figure characters—and has it delivered to a certain lodger, another American national at a nearby farm.
While waiting for the result of this message, the detective explains to the companion and the local inspector how he cracked the code of the dancing figures.
In his explanation, the detective discusses what happened after he cracked the third message.

He sent a telegram inquiry to a friend of his in the police of an overseas city concerning the lodger, whose name was in the first message, and received a reply stating that the lodger was a deadly criminal from another overseas city.
The detective decoded the lodger's first three messages as: "AM HERE – THE LODGER," "AT THE FARMER'S" (the name of the farm at which he was staying), and "COME WIFE."
A short fourth message proved to be a response from the wife: "NEVER."
The last message from the lodger, which prompted the detective and the companion to rush to the county, read "WIFE PREPARE TO MEET THY GOD."
The lodger, unaware that the wife is gravely wounded, arrives at the manor house and is seized as he comes through the door.
The detective had sent for the lodger using the dancing men, knowing that the lodger would believe the message was from the wife.
The lodger reveals that he had been engaged to the wife, the daughter of the crime boss of that other overseas city for whom the lodger works, and that she had fled to escape her old life.
The lodger had come to this country to get her back.
When the lodger and the wife were speaking through a window, the squire had appeared and shots were exchanged; the squire was killed and the lodger had fled.
Apparently, the wife then shot herself.
The lodger is arrested and sentenced to hang, but his sentence is reduced to penal servitude because the squire had fired the first shot.
The wife recovers from her injuries, and spends her life helping the poor and administering her late husband's estate.
The detective is contacted by the young woman of a country town in the rural county about an unusual turn in her and her mother's lives.
The young woman's father has recently died and left his wife and daughter rather poor.
There was an ad in the news asking about their whereabouts.
Answering it, they met the employer and the ruffian, the former a pleasant enough man, but the latter a bullying churl.
They had come from a distant colony, where they had known the young woman's uncle, who had now also died in poverty and apparently wanted to see that his relatives were provided for.
This struck the young woman as odd, since she and her family had not heard a word from the uncle since his departure for the distant colony 25 years ago.
The employer and the ruffian explained that before dying, the uncle had heard of his brother's death and felt responsible for his survivors' welfare.
The employer began by offering the young woman a job as a live-in music teacher for his ten-year-old daughter at £100 a year, about twice the going rate.
She accepted after the employer said that she could visit her mother on weekends.
That went well until the ruffian came to stay for a week.
He made the most oafish advances to her, and boasted that if the young woman married him she would have a life of luxury.
He even grabbed her and demanded a kiss, precipitating expulsion by his host, the employer.
The young woman has not seen the ruffian since.

The specific thing that has brought the young woman to seek the detective's services, however, is the strange man who follows her on his bicycle as she cycles to and from the railway station for her weekend visits to her mother.
The strange man always keeps his distance behind her and disappears without a trace, never letting her near him, and always along the same lonely stretch of road.
The young woman does not recognise him, but he has a black beard.

The detective asks her about her admirers, and other than the ruffian, if he can be styled as such, she can only think of the employer, who, although a perfect gentleman at all times, seems attracted to her.
After the young woman leaves, the detective observes that it is odd that a household would pay £100 a year for a music teacher but be too cheap to pay for a horse and trap.
He sends the companion to the rural county to see what he can find out.
This turns out to be virtually nothing, except to establish that the lady's story is true, and that the mystery man comes out of and goes back into a local house, the old hall.
The detective upbraids the companion for his lackluster results.

They also receive a letter from the young woman the next day saying that the employer has proposed to her, but she had to refuse since she is already engaged to a certain man, an electrical engineer in an industrial city.

The detective goes to the rural county himself, and gets into a fight in a pub for his troubles; when he returns and tells the companion what happened, he actually considers his experience in the rural county to be hilarious.
It seems that the ruffian was in the taproom at the pub and heard his name mentioned in conversation.
He came out and demanded to know who the detective was and what he wanted.
The discussion escalated to violence; the detective emerged with a few bruises, whereas the ruffian had to be carried home.
The innkeeper merely mentioned that the ruffian is a regular weekend guest at the old hall, which is rented by the tenant, who, rumour has it, is a clergyman.

The detective returns to his lodgings with his face somewhat marred, and another letter arrives from the young woman, saying that her situation has become impossible owing to the employer's proposals, and the ruffian's reappearance.
She is quitting.
The detective knows that some intrigue is afoot, and he tells the companion that they must get themselves to the rural county to see that the young woman makes it to the station.
The employer has at last acquired a trap, and she need not ride her bicycle this time.
Failing to realise that the young woman might take an earlier train than usual, the detective discovers that he is too late to meet the young woman.
The trap comes along the road, but by the time it does, no one is in it: the young woman has been abducted.
The detective and the companion board the empty trap in an attempt to go after the kidnappers.
They come face-to-face with the mysterious cyclist, who pulls a revolver on them; however, both parties quickly realise that they are on the same side – both have the young woman's welfare in mind.
The cyclist declares that the abductors are the ruffian and the tenant.
He evidently knows something of the intrigue.

The group first find an unconscious groom, who was driving the trap, in the bushes, and then they find all three persons that they have been seeking on the old hall grounds, with the apparently defrocked clergyman performing a wedding ceremony between the other two.
The bride is somewhat unwilling, judging from the gag over her mouth.
The ruffian's boast of having married the young woman leads the mysterious cyclist, unmasking himself as the employer, to pull out his revolver and shoot the ruffian, wounding him.
The detective receives a visit from the schoolmaster, the founder and principal of a preparatory school called the boarding school in the north of the country.
He beseeches the detective to come back to the town with him to look into the disappearance of one of his pupils, the ten-year-old young lord, whose father is the very rich and famous Duke.
The schoolmaster explains that not only the boy has disappeared, but also the German master, the teacher, along with his bicycle.
Once in the north, the Duke says to the detective that he does not think that his estranged wife has anything to do with his son's disappearance, nor has there been a ransom demand.
The detective establishes that the boy and his kidnappers could not have used the nearby road without being seen, suggesting that they went cross-country.
As if to confirm this, the police find the boy's school cap in some gypsies' possession.
They swear that they simply found it on the moor, but the police lock them up.
The detective and the doctor go hunting for clues.
They find a bicycle track, but it is not the teacher's; it does not match his tyres.
The detective observes that one tyre has a patch on it.
Almost everything observable has been obliterated by cow tracks (which are the only marks on the ground anywhere).
Eventually, the teacher's bicycle tracks are found, and they end where he lies, dead.

After that, the detective and the doctor arrive at the inn, and meet the innkeeper, the landlord, who seems startled indeed to hear that the detective wants to go to the hall, the Duke's nearby house, to tell him news of his son.
The two men have lunch there, and the detective suddenly realises that he and the doctor saw many cow tracks out on the moor, but never at any time did they see any cows.
Furthermore, the patterns of the hoof prints were quite unusual, suggesting that the cow in question trotted, cantered, and galloped.
The detective and the doctor sneak out to the landlord's stable and examine the horse's hooves.
As the detective has expected, there is evidence of recent shoeing, but with old shoes and new nails.
Examining the nearby smithy, the detective and the doctor are rather belligerently asked to leave by the landlord.
Shortly afterwards, the two men hide as a cyclist comes along the road from the direction of the Duke's.
It is the secretary, the Duke's personal secretary, and he looks agitated.
He arrives at the inn.
Soon afterwards, a trap pulls out of the stable yard and goes along the road towards the neighbouring town.
A while later, someone else – it is getting dark and only a fleeting glimpse of the new visitor is caught – arrives at the inn.
Coming closer, the detective observes the secretary's bicycle tyres and notes that they are the same make as the first ones encountered on the moor.
The next morning, they go to the hall, where they find that the Duke is not well.
Nevertheless, the detective demands from him a cheque for £6000, saying that he has earned the reward.
His son is at the inn, and the accused is the Duke himself, but the actual mastermind of this crime is the secretary, who has a terrible secret: He is the illegitimate son of the Duke.
He conceived a plan to kidnap the young lord to force the Duke to change his will, knowing very well that his father would not call the police on him, as he abhorred the very idea of scandal.
The plan had begun to unravel when the secretary hired the landlord – who has now fled, but been caught on the detective's information – to do the actual kidnapping.
The landlord had killed the teacher, and when the secretary heard the news, he confessed all to his father.
So anxious had been the Duke to avoid scandal, he agreed to let his younger son remain confined at the inn for another three days, and to keep quiet, so that the landlord could flee justice.
All ends well, except for the landlord, who faces the gallows.
The young lord is brought home from the inn and the Duke writes to his estranged wife asking her to reconcile with him.
This he feels she will be willing to do, for the source of the friction between them is going away: the secretary is being packed off to a distant country to seek his fortune.
As for the cow tracks, they were accomplished by shoeing the horses with special shoes shaped like cow's hooves.
The shoes were from the Duke's collection of family memorabilia.
The story ends with the detective receiving the £6000 reward from the Duke for his services, joking "I am a poor man".
The next story, "the tale of a sea captain", confirms that such a large payment is very unusual for the detective.
A village in the wooded countryside is the scene of a harpoon murder, and a young police inspector, the young officer, asks the detective, whom he admires, for help.
The detective has already determined that it would take a great deal of strength and skill to run a man through with a harpoon and embed it in the wall behind him.
The captain, the 50-year-old victim and former master of the whaler of a northern port, who lived with his wife and daughter, had a reputation for being violent.
The captain did not sleep in the family house, but in a small hut that he built some distance from the house, whose interior he had decorated to look like a sailor's cabin on a ship.
This is where he was found harpooned.
The young officer could find no footprints or other physical evidence.
However, a tobacco pouch made of sealskin and with initials that match the captain's was found at the scene, full of strong ship's tobacco.
This is rather unusual, as the captain—or "the black captain" as people called him—seldom smoked.
Indeed, the young officer found no pipe in the cabin.
The captain was found fully dressed, suggesting that he was expecting a visitor, and there was some rum laid out along with two dirty glasses.
There were brandy and whisky, too, but neither had been touched.
There was also a knife in its sheath at the captain's feet; the captain's wife has identified it as her husband's.
A little notebook was also found at the scene.
It contains a first initial.
A second initial and the year 1883.
An abbreviation on the second page, which the detective reckons stands for a railway company.
The first set of initials is likely a stockbroker's, as the little book is full of what appears to be stock exchange information.
The detective decides to accompany the young officer to the village and, upon arrival, the young officer observes that someone has recently tried to break into the captain's cabin, but failed.
After examining the inside of the cabin, the detective deduces from the lack of dust that something has been taken from a shelf, even though the burglar did not get in.
The stolen item was a book, or possibly a box.
The detective believes that the burglar will likely try again, this time bringing a more useful tool for the job.
So, the detective, the doctor, and the young officer all lie in wait for the burglar that night, and they are not disappointed.
Along he comes, m breaks into the cabin, and goes through one of the captain's old logbooks, cursing when he finds that the information that he wants is missing, having been torn out of the book.
As he is leaving the cabin, the young officer moves in and arrests him.
He is the young man—whose name matches the initials in the notebook—the son of a long-vanished, failed banker.
He claims he was looking at the captain's logs to test a theory of his.
His father disappeared with a box full of securities after his bank failed.
He took them on a yacht bound for a northern country.
He believes that his father's boat may have been driven north in the northern sea by bad weather, and met the whaler, captained by the captain.

He believes that the captain knew something about his father's disappearance, and that possibly his father was murdered by the man who has now himself become a murder victim as he has traced some of his father's long lost securities back to the captain.
The young officer takes the young man off to the station, even though the young man swears that he has nothing to do with the murder.
The detective believes this to be true, because the young man is a slight, anaemic thin man, hardly capable of running a man through with a harpoon.
The detective saves the young man from the noose by finding the true killer in a most unusual way.
He advertises for a harpooner, posing as a sea captain under a false name.

He gets three applicants at his lodgings for the job, and one of them is indeed the captain's killer, as confirmed by his name, with its matching initials, and the fact that the detective had established that he was once the captain's shipmate.
The detective also felt sure that a murderer would want to leave the country for a while.
The detective handcuffs the unaware harpooner after which the harpooner confesses.
While he freely admits to killing the captain, he furiously denies that it was murder, claiming self-defence.
He was actually at the captain's cabin to extort hush money from him.

The young man's father had indeed come aboard the whaler with his tin box of securities, and the captain had murdered him by throwing him overboard while he believed no-one was looking, though the harpooner had secretly witnessed the event.

The detective is hired by the débutante, the young lady, to retrieve compromising letters from a blackmailer: the extortioner, who causes the detective more revulsion than any of the 50-odd murderers in his career.
The extortioner is "the king of blackmailers".
He demands £7,000 (£763,572 in 2025) for the letters, which if given to third parties would cause a scandal that would end the young lady's marriage engagement.
The detective offers £2,000, all the young lady can pay, but the extortioner insists on £7,000.

It is worth £7,000 to him, he explains, to make an example of the young lady; it is in his long-term interest to ensure that his future blackmail victims would be more "open to reason" and pay him what he wants, knowing he will destroy them if they do not.
The detective resolves to recover the letters by whatever means necessary, as the extortioner has placed himself outside the bounds of morality.
The detective visits the extortioner's suburban house, disguised as a plumber, in order to learn the plan of the house and the extortioner's daily routine.
He cultivates the acquaintance of the extortioner's housemaid and even becomes engaged to marry her.
This rather shocks the doctor, but the detective assures him that he has a hated rival who will step in when the plumber disappears.
The detective has learned where the extortioner keeps his blackmail papers (a safe in his study), and plans to burgle the extortioner's house that night.
The doctor comes along.
They break into the study, but just as the detective opens the safe, the extortioner enters the study, even though he should be in bed asleep.
The detective and the doctor hide behind a curtain, while the extortioner has a midnight meeting with a supposed maidservant offering to sell letters that would compromise her mistress.
The woman is actually one of the extortioner's former victims, whose broken-hearted husband died when she wouldn't pay the extortioner and he revealed her secret.
Now she avenges her husband by shooting the extortioner to death, then stamps on his face.
The doctor instinctively begins to rush out and stop the shooting, but the detective restrains him.
The detective understands, and the doctor instantly realises, "that it was no affair of ours; that justice had overtaken a villain..."
The woman runs away, and the extortioner's household is roused by the shots.
During his final confrontation, the extortioner's entire cache of blackmail papers had been in a safe with its door slightly ajar.
The detective now feeds this mass of compromising material into the extortioner's burning fireplace, despite the risk of being discovered and caught.
Then the detective and the doctor escape through the garden and over the wall.
The doctor has to kick himself free from a pursuer who has grabbed his leg.

The next morning, the inspector calls at the detective's lodgings to ask for the detective's help in investigating the extortioner's murder, which he ascribes to the two burglars seen escaping over the garden wall.
He has a description of one of them: "a middle-aged, strongly built man-square jaw, thick neck, moustache..."
The detective calls the description vague, and even jokes that it could describe the doctor, which amuses the inspector.
But the detective refuses the inspector's request, stating that he sympathizes with the criminals rather than the victim.
Later, the detective recognises the face of the woman who killed the extortioner.
He shows the doctor her photograph displayed in a shop-window among those of other celebrities.
The doctor recognises the name of her famous husband, but the detective signals silence with a finger to his lips.
The doctor assures his readers that the killer in question is beyond the reach of the law [i.e. deceased] and that certain details have been disguised to hurt no one.
The inspector of the city police brings the detective a mysterious problem about a man who shatters plaster busts of the emperor.
One was shattered in the shopkeeper's shop, and two others, sold by the shopkeeper to a physician, were smashed after the doctor's house and branch office had been burgled.
Nothing else was taken.
In the former case, the bust was taken outside before being broken.
The detective knows that the inspector's theory about an emperor-hating lunatic must be wrong.
The busts in question all came from the same mould, when there are thousands of images of the emperor all over the city.
The next day, the inspector calls the detective to a house where there has been yet another bust-shattering, but there has also been a murder.
The householder found the dead man on his doorstep after investigating a noise.
His emperor bust was also taken by a burglar entering through a window.
It, too, was from the same mould.
Also, a photograph of a rather ape-ish-looking man is found in the dead man's pocket.
The fragments of the householder's bust are in the front garden of an empty house up the street.

The detective concludes that the burglar wanted to see what he was doing, for there is a streetlamp here, whereas the bust could have been broken at another empty house nearer the householder's, but it had been dark there.
The detective tells the inspector to tell the householder, a journalist for a press agency, that he is convinced that the culprit is a lunatic.
The detective knows that this is not true, but it is expedient to use the press to convince the culprit that this is what the investigators believe.
The detective interviews the two shopkeepers who sold the busts and finds out whom they were sold to, and where they were made, the sculpture works.
A couple of his informants also recognise the ape-ish man in the picture.
They know him as the labourer, an Italian immigrant.
He even worked in the shop where the first bust was broken, having left his job there only two days earlier.

The detective goes to the sculpture works and finds out that the busts were part of a batch of six, but other than that, the manager can think of no reason why they should be special, or why anyone would want to destroy them.
He recognises the labourer's picture, and describes him as a rascal.
He was imprisoned for a street-fight stabbing a year earlier, but has likely been released now.
He once worked at the sculpture works, but has not been back.
His cousin still works there.
The detective begs the manager not to talk to the cousin about the labourer.
That evening, the inspector brings news that the dead man has been identified as the gangster, a Mafioso.
The inspector believes that the gangster was sent to kill the culprit, but wound up dead himself.
After sending an express message, the detective invites his companion and the inspector to join him outside a house in a suburb where apparently the detective is expecting another bust-breaking.
The inspector by now is exasperated with the detective's preoccupation with the busts, but comes.
They are not disappointed.
The labourer shows up, enters the house, and comes back out of the window minutes later with an emperor bust, which he proceeds to shatter.
He then examines the pieces, quite unaware that the detective and the inspector are sneaking up behind him.
They pounce, and the labourer is arrested.
He will not talk, however.

The mystery is at last laid bare after the detective offers £10 (£ in ) to the owner of the last existing bust, making him sign a document transferring all rights and ownership of the bust to the detective.
After the seller has left, the detective smashes the bust with a hunting crop.
Among the plaster shards is a gem, the black pearl of a noble family.
The detective was aware of the case of its disappearance from the beginning.
Suspicion had fallen on the owner's maid, whose surname was the gangster's – the dead man's sister.
The labourer somehow got the pearl from the gangster, and hid it inside a still-soft plaster bust at the factory where he worked, moments before his arrest for the street-fight stabbing.
The detective and the doctor find themselves in a university town when a tutor and lecturer of one of the colleges, the don, brings him an interesting problem.
The don had been reviewing the galley proofs of an exam he was going to give when he left his office for an hour.

When he returned, he found that his servant, the manservant, had entered the room but accidentally left his key in the lock when he left, and someone had disturbed the exam papers on his desk and left traces that show it had been partially copied.
The manservant is devastated and collapses on a chair, but swears that he did not touch the papers.
The don found other clues in his office: pencil shavings, a broken pencil lead, a fresh cut in his desk surface, and a small blob of black clay speckled with sawdust.
The don wants to uncover the cheater and prevent him from taking the exam, since it is for a sizeable scholarship.
Three students who will take the exam live above him in the same building.

The first, the tall student, is athletic, being a hurdler and a long-jumper, and industrious (in contrast to his father who squandered his fortune in horse racing); the second, another student, is described as quiet and methodical; the third is a further student, a gifted man but thoroughly dissolute and given to gambling.
The detective examines the office.
The cheater obviously took the papers over to the window one by one while he copied them so that he could see the don returning, but as it happens, the don did not come back the usual way.
A nearby door leads to the don's bedroom.
Upon examining that, the detective finds another, similar, sawdust-speckled blob of clay.
He stuns the don by telling him that the cheater, upon hearing his approach, hid in the don's bedroom.
He was there, hiding behind a curtain, all the time that the don was questioning the manservant.
The next morning, the detective and the doctor return to the don's office.
The detective confronts the manservant, accusing him of withholding information.
The manservant will not own up to anything, and insists that there was no one in the don's office while he was there.
The detective, however, sends for the tall student, and proceeds to lay out his results.
The cheater was someone who knew the exam proofs were there.
This could only be the tall student, because the proofs' whereabouts had been kept secret, and the tall student was the only one tall enough to look in through the don's window to see his desk.
The detective has also identified the blobs as the special clay found in the long-jump pit, further implicating the tall student.
The tall student reveals his guilt by reproaching the manservant for his apparent treachery.
The manservant was indeed the one who covered for the tall student.
He felt that he had to, for old times' sake: the manservant was once the tall student's father's butler.
The detective then explains the remaining clues.
The scratch on the desk was caused by the tall student's spiked jumping shoes as he grabbed them in his haste, and the clay blobs fell from his shoes.
The manservant had collapsed in the chair to hide the tall student's gloves, which he saw had been left on the chair.

For his part, the tall student credits the manservant with convincing him not to profit from his misdeed, and presents the don with a letter stating his wish not to sit the exam, but to instead accept an offer to work for a colonial police force.
One wretched November night, the inspector visits the detective at his lodgings to discuss the violent death of the young man, secretary to the aged invalid professor.
The professor had dismissed his previous two secretaries.
The murder happened at a country house near a town in the neighbouring county, the fatal weapon being a sealing-wax knife belonging to the professor.
The inspector can identify no motive for the killing, with the young man having no enemies or trouble in his past.
The young man was found by the professor's maid, who recounts his last words as "The professor; it was she."

The maid further told the inspector that before the murder, she heard the young man leave his room and walk down to the study; she had been hanging curtains and did not see him, only recognising his brisk step.
The professor was in bed at the time.
A minute later, a hoarse scream issued from the study, and the maid, hesitating briefly, entered and found the murder.
She later tells the detective that the young man went out for a walk not long before the murder.

The murderer's only likely means of entry was through the back door after walking along the path from the road, and the inspector found some indistinct footmarks running beside the path, the murderer obviously seeking to leave no trail.
The inspector could not tell whether the track was coming or going, nor whether made by big or small feet.
The professor's study contained a bureau; nothing seemed to have been stolen.
Its drawers were left open, as was normal, and the cupboard in the middle was locked.
The professor kept the key.
A lone piece of evidence was found in the young man's hand: a pair of golden pince-nez spectacles.

The detective examines these and from them alone deduces the following details of the murderer: It is a woman; She is of some good breeding; She dresses like a lady; She is a person of refinement and is well dressed; She has a thick nose; Her eyes are close together; She has a puckered forehead, a peering look, and likely rounded shoulders; She has been to an optician at least twice over the last few months.
The detective, the doctor, and the inspector head to the country house the next morning, and the detective carefully examines the site.
In the study, he notices a recent scratch on the bureau and reasons the murderer intended to access its contents.
The young man was killed as his presence interfered with the burglary.
No-one saw the murderer leave, nor did anyone hear a door opening.
The detective notes that both the corridors, the one leading from the back door and the one leading to the professor's bedroom, are about the same length and lined with coconut matting.
The detective interviews the professor in his bedroom, smoking many Egyptian cigarettes and dropping the ashes all over the floor.
The professor claims utter ignorance regarding the murder and ventures that the young man's death may be suicide.
The detective asks about the locked cupboard in the bureau.
The professor hands over the key.
The detective inspects the key and returns it immediately, leaving the bureau sealed.
The doctor asks the detective if he has a clue, and the detective tells him the cigarette ashes might reveal the truth.
The detective meets the housekeeper in the garden and has a seemingly unimportant conversation about the professor's eating habits; apparently, he has eaten heavily today.
In the afternoon, the three men return to the professor in his room, and the detective deliberately knocks the cigarettes over as an excuse to get a closer look at the floor.
The detective's suspicion is confirmed – there are footprints in the ash.
At that moment, the murderer, appearing exactly as the detective deduced, emerges from a hiding place in a bookcase.
The mystery's explanation is revealed as: the woman came in secret to the professor's house to obtain some documents, using a duplicate key she gained from one of the former secretaries.
She was surprised by the young man, whom she attacked with the nearest object to hand, the sealing-wax knife; she had not intended to kill him.
She lost her pince-nez in the scramble to escape; unable to see clearly, she turned along the wrong corridor and wound up in the professor's room.
Although surprised, he hid her.
The murderer is, in fact, the professor's estranged wife, the woman, and they are both Russian.
Years prior, the pair had been involved with nihilists; she and a non-violent nihilist friend were both betrayed by the professor for gain.
Having finished her jail sentence in a remote region, the woman came in search of evidence that would exonerate her friend.
The woman had met the young man while he was taking his walk, explaining the young man's last words.
The professor's increased appetite is, of course, explained by his having to feed a second, hidden person.
The team leader of a college, in the university town, comes to the detective seeking his help in the missing player's disappearance.

The missing player is the star player on the team leader's rugby union team (who plays at the three-quarters position, hence the story's title) and they will likely lose an important match the following day against the rival university if the missing player cannot be found.
The detective has to admit that amateur sport is outside his field of expertise, but he shows the same care he has shown to his other cases.
The missing player had seemed a bit pale and bothered earlier in the day.

Later in the evening, according to a hotel porter, a rough-looking, bearded man came to the hotel with a note for the missing player; judging from the young man's reaction, the note contained rather devastating news.
He immediately left the hotel with the bearded stranger; the two of them were last seen running in the direction of a main street at about half past ten.
No one has seen them since.
The team leader has wired to the university town, but the missing player has not been seen there.
He has also wired the nobleman, the missing player's very wealthy uncle and nearest living relative, but has heard no answer.
The missing player is the almost-eighty-year-old nobleman's heir, but he must meanwhile live in relative poverty owing to his uncle's miserly behaviour.
The detective further questions the porter.

The bearded man who brought the note was neither a gentleman nor a workman, and he seemed to be bothered by something too, for his hand was trembling as he handed the porter the note to give to the missing player.
The only word that the porter overheard of their short conversation was "time".
Earlier in the evening, at six o'clock, the porter had brought the missing player a telegram, and saw the missing player write a reply.
The missing player told the porter that he would send it himself.
The detective looks at the telegraph forms in the missing player's room, and then at the blotter, finally finding a clue.
The impression on the blotter yields a part of the message that the missing player sent: "Stand by us for God's sake".
Obviously at least one other person is involved ("us"), and there is some kind of danger.
The nobleman briefly visits, but can give the detective no useful information as to his nephew's whereabouts.
The old miser seems utterly aghast at the possibility that it might be a kidnapping whose object would be to extort his wealth.
The detective and his companion then go to the telegraph office, where the detective uses a ruse to get the woman there to show him the counterfoil of the message that the missing player sent.
It was addressed to the physician, a medical academic at the university town.
The detective and his companion go to see the physician, who tells them that the missing player is an intimate friend of his.
He does not react when told that the missing player has disappeared, and claims not to know where he is, and not to have seen him recently.

However, when the detective produces a bill for services issued by the physician to the missing player, the physician furiously refuses to answer any more questions, denies that he had the telegram from the missing player, and has his butler show the detective and his companion out.
The detective deduces that the physician must know where the missing player is, and lodges at an inn just across the street from the physician's office to keep watch.
The detective learns that the physician, although not in actual medical practice, regularly rides in his brougham out into the country somewhere.
The round trip seems to take about three hours.
The detective tries following the brougham on one of its outings, but is thwarted by the physician, who makes it quite clear that he is aware that the detective is following him.
The next day, the detective's inquiries in all the local villages come to naught; no one has seen the doctor's brougham passing through.
The mystery is at last unlocked by the hound, a beagle-foxhound cross.
After the detective covertly sprays aniseed oil onto the wheels of the doctor's brougham, the hound tracks it to a cottage in the countryside.
What the detective finds there is not pleasant.
The missing player is there, but is grieving over his young wife, who has just died of consumption.
Her existence was kept secret, because the nobleman would not have approved of the marriage and would have disowned his nephew.
The physician had told the woman's father about her condition, and he, the bearded stranger, had unwisely told the missing player, who felt compelled to rush off forthwith.
The detective tells the physician that as long as there is no foul play involved, private affairs are not his business.
He and his companion then depart, leaving the missing player to his grief.
The detective wakes up the doctor early one winter morning to rush to a murder scene at the country house near a town in the county.
The master of the house has been killed, apparently by burglars.
The inspector believes that it was the infamous local gang who have committed several other burglaries in the neighbourhood.
At the country house, the lady of the house tells the detective that her marriage was not happy; the master of the house was a violent, abusive drunkard.
She then tells that about 11 o'clock, in the dining room, she encountered an elderly man coming in the French window, followed by two younger men.
The older man struck her in the face, knocking her out.
When she came to, she was gagged and tied to an oaken chair with the bellrope, which they had torn down.
The master of the house came into the room and rushed at the intruders, one of whom struck and killed him with a poker.
The lady of the house fainted again for a minute or two.
She saw the intruders drinking wine from a bottle taken from the sideboard.
Then they left, taking some silver plate.
The master of the house's corpse is still lying at the murder scene.
The inspector tells the detective some unsavoury things about the master of the house: that he poured petroleum over his wife's dog and set it alight, and once threw a decanter at her maid.
The maid corroborates the lady of the house's account of the master of the house being an abusive alcoholic.
Examining the bellrope, the detective notes that if it was tugged hard enough to tear it down, the bell would have rung in the kitchen, and asks why nobody heard it.
The inspector answers that it was late, and the kitchen is at the back of the house, where none of the servants would have heard.
This suggests that the burglars must have known this, indicating a link between them and one of the servants.
Oddly, the thieves stole only a few items of silver plate from the dining room.

The half-empty wine bottle and glasses interest the detective – the cork had been drawn with the corkscrew of a "multiplex knife", not the long corkscrew in the drawer, and one of the glasses has beeswing dregs in it, but the others have none.
Annoyed at being called to investigate a case that apparently has a ready-made solution, the detective decides to catch the train back to the city.

However, after having mulled things over during the journey, the detective thinks that the lady of the house's story has too many holes in it and that probably she and the maid have lied deliberately, staging a false crime scene.

Upon returning to the country house, the detective, after examining again the supposed crime scene, reaches this conclusion: the killer cut the bellrope with a knife, and frayed the loose end to make it look broken.
The detective confronts the lady of the house and the maid, telling them he knows they are lying and demanding the truth, but they stand by their story.
On the way out, the detective notices a hole in the ice on the pond, and writes a note for the inspector.

The detective searches for the killer: almost certainly a sailor (indicated by the knots and the active physique) who was previously acquainted with the lady of the house, and whom she and the maid would protect.
The lady of the house travelled by the ocean liner of a shipping line, which is now halfway to the far-off country.
However, the ship's first officer, the seaman, who has been promoted to captain, has remained in the country and in two days will take command of the company's new ship, another vessel.
The detective takes a cab to police headquarters but does not go in.
He tells the doctor he is reluctant to name the criminal to the police until he knows more.
That evening, the inspector calls at the detective's lodgings, with two items of news: As suggested in the detective's note, the stolen silver was found at the bottom of the pond.
The detective suggests that the theft was a blind—a deliberate false clue.
However, the inspector rationalises that the pond was chosen as a temporary hiding place.
The local gang was arrested in a foreign city that morning, so they couldn't have committed a murder in the county the previous night.
Later that evening, the seaman comes to the detective's lodgings, summoned by a telegram from the detective.
The detective demands a full account of what happened at the country house, warning the seaman that the detective will summon the police if he lies or conceals anything.
The seaman met a woman, the young lady (the lady of the house), on the voyage from the far-off country.
He fell in love with her, but not she with him.
Then he happened to meet the maid, who told him of the master of the house's abusive behaviour.
He met secretly with the young lady at the house; the last time on the previous night.
They were in the dining room when the master of the house burst in, insulted the young lady, and struck her with a cudgel.
